ta-l1d30q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 30. Having shown that 'principle' with respect to creatures is said of God from time, Lombard shows how something can be said of God from time: first that it is, answering an objection, and then the manner, namely without change in God and without a real relation, the name alone being relative. From this he solves a question left open in Dist. 18. Three articles are announced: whether anything is said of God from time; whether such names signify the divine essence; and whether these relative names posit a relation really existing in God.
claims: Names said of God from time imply no change and no real relation in God.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e118.summary: First argument that nothing is said of God from time. What newly comes to be said of something can be said to have become so, as a man becomes white, and becoming does not fit God any more than change, since he is the first mover.
claims: New predication implies becoming.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e121.summary: Second argument. A predicate is said per se or per accidens. Not per se, since what is per se is always present, and these are not said of God eternally; not per accidens, since there is no accident in God, and every per accidens reduces to something per se, so these would be per se of something else, which is not found, since nothing but God is Creator or Lord of the universe.
claims: Temporal names are neither per se nor per accidens.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens predication

ta-l1d30q1-d1e124.summary: Third argument, against the reply that this is predication by cause. Such predication can be resolved into a proposition denoting the causal relation, as 'God is our hope' into 'our hope is from God', but 'the Creator is from God' cannot be said.
claims: 'Creator' is not causal predication.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e128.summary: Fourth argument. Everything true is necessary or contingent. These are not predicated of God necessarily, since not always, nor contingently, since nothing in God is contingent.
claims: Temporal names are neither necessary nor contingent.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e131.summary: Sed contra from everything said in the text by Augustine and Lombard, common usage, faith, and philosophy.
claims: Some things are said of God from time.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e134.summary: Thomas's determination. Something must be said of God from time. Since all being of each thing, of the universe and each part, flows from God, he must be designated in the relation of principle to each thing, and since many things have not always existed, even if the universe had always existed, as some philosophers wrongly held, names designating this relation are said of God from time, not eternally, since a relation in act requires both extremes in act, and God can be referred to a creature as its actual principle only when the creature actually exists. This does not happen with absolute names, which by their concepts posit something in their subject, like quantity and quality, so they are really in God and cannot be said of something from time without its changing by receiving what it lacked. But relation by its concept posits nothing in its subject, only a respect to another, so some relation does not really exist in its subject (Dist. 26), and such relations come to be said of something anew not by its change but by the change of what it is referred to, as with everything said of God from time.
claims: Relations to creatures are said of God from time, since a relation in act needs both extremes.
Relations can be newly said without change in their subject, unlike absolute predicates.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e137.summary: Reply to the first argument. As these relations are in God only conceptually, so their being newly said implies no real becoming in God, only conceptual, as Ps. 89:1 says 'Lord, you have become our refuge'. Even if it is granted that he has become something conceptually, such as refuge, he must in no way be called changed, since 'change' refers to departure from the starting point and 'becoming' to attaining the end, and nothing departs from God even if a conceptual relation comes to him.
claims: God 'becomes' refuge only conceptually and is in no way changed.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e143.summary: Reply to the second argument. According to Lombard these are predicated per accidens, not as being in God but in creatures. Two things should be considered: the relations themselves and their foundation in God, as the relation of creation is founded on the divine power to bring things into being from nothing. As to their foundation, they are said per se and belong to God eternally, since essence, power, and operation are eternal. As to the relation itself, they are said per accidens. 'Accident' means either a nature divided against substance, and so nothing in God is accidental, or what belongs through another, as the white builds per accidens because it is joined to the builder, and in this sense it belongs to God per accidens to be referred to something outside him, since he is called relative only because another is referred to him, as the knowable is relative (the Philosopher). It does not follow that the relation designated in God belongs to something else per se, but rather that the opposite respect does, being a creature or a servant.
claims: As to their foundation, temporal names are per se and eternal; as to the relation, per accidens.
God is called relative because creatures are referred to him.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e146.summary: Reply to the third argument. This cannot properly be called predication by cause, unless such names are understood to predicate the relation of some cause.
claims: Temporal names predicate a causal relation, not by cause.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. As said in reply to the second, they are predicated necessarily in the way they are per se and contingently in the way they are per accidens, but it does not follow that anything contingent is in God.
claims: Contingency lies in the relation, not in God.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e162.summary: First argument that names said of God from time do not signify the divine essence. The essence is eternal and these are not said eternally.
claims: Temporal names are not eternal.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e165.summary: Second argument. God is called from time our patience and our hope, which carry imperfection and cannot fit the divine essence, unlike charity, whose concept has no imperfection.
claims: Patience and hope imply imperfection.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e168.summary: Third argument. The essence is common to the three, but some temporal names do not fit all three, like 'sent' and 'given'.
claims: Missus and donatus are personal.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e172.summary: Fourth argument. God is called man from time, and 'man' signifies human nature, which in the Incarnation was not mixed with the divine nature but remained distinct from it.
claims: 'Man' signifies human, not divine, nature.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e175.summary: Sed contra. The masters say every name connoting an effect in creatures signifies the divine essence, and temporal names are said with respect to creatures.
claims: Names connoting effects signify essence.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e178.summary: Second sed contra. Dionysius says every beneficent name of God, whichever person it is said of, should be taken of the whole deity, and all names implying relation to creatures name some benefit in them.
claims: Beneficent names belong to the whole deity.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e181.summary: Thomas's determination. Nothing is said of God from time except what implies a relation to creatures, which can be designated as the creature refers to God as principle or as term. As principle, either something is properly predicated of God designating the relation of principle to principled, or something designating the effect itself, as in predication by cause ('God is our hope'). In the first case, sometimes a name is imposed to signify the relation itself, like 'Lord', relative by being, which signifies first the relation that is conceptually in God and consequently the essence on which it is founded; sometimes to signify the foundation of the relation, as 'knowledge' signifies a quality followed by a respect to the knowable, relative only by being said, which principally signify a thing of another category and consequently imply relation. So in God 'Creator' is imposed to signify the divine action, which is the essence, followed by a relation to creatures, and principally signifies the essence and consequently implies the relation. Predication by cause is similar, resolving into causal relations ('God is our patience', i.e. its cause). All temporal names implying the relation of principle to principled belong to the whole Trinity. As term, the creature's relation may be to something essential or personal, in three ways: by operation, as one can understand or name God or paternity; by exemplarity, as creation terminates in the likeness of essential attributes and the infusion of charity in the likeness of the Spirit's personal procession; or by being, uniquely in the Incarnation, by which human nature is assumed into the being and unity of a divine person, not the divine nature. The relation to God as term includes consequently the relation to him as principle. So in names said by the creature's relation to God as term, as to the term they can belong only to a person, but as to the included principle they belong to the whole Trinity, giving understanding of the person by one relation and of the essence by the other, as only the Son is incarnate, since the Incarnation terminated in him alone, though the whole Trinity effected it.
claims: Temporal names relating God as principle belong to the whole Trinity and signify the essence principally or consequently.
Names relating God as term can belong to one person, by operation, exemplarity, or being (the Incarnation), while including the Trinity as principle.
concepts: God as principle and as term
relativa secundum esse vs. secundum dici

ta-l1d30q1-d1e184.summary: Reply to the first argument. Such names belong to God from time by reason of the relation they imply, principally (as the text reads, when 'Deus' is said) or consequently (as with 'Creator'). That relation is not in the divine essence or any thing in God, but by the essence on which it is founded such names belong to God eternally, as it were habitually.
claims: Temporal names belong to God eternally as to their foundation, habitually.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the second argument. God's essence is not patience or hope, nor does 'God is our hope' signify this, but rather the causal relation of the divine essence to such an effect in us, and so with the others.
claims: 'God is our hope' signifies a causal relation.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e191.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Sent', 'incarnate', and the like imply two relations, of term and of principle. The relation of principle belongs to the whole Trinity, so we say the whole Trinity sends or effects the Incarnation, but the other belongs to a determinate person, so such names are not said of the whole Trinity.
claims: Mission names include a Trinitarian principle and a personal term.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e194.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God is called man inasmuch as a supposit of the divine nature, the Son, subsists in human nature by union. This union is a relation really existing in the assumed creature, which as to term terminates in the person of the Son, in whom the union was made, and as to principle refers to the whole Trinity, which made the union.
claims: The hypostatic union is a real relation in the creature, terminating in the Son and caused by the Trinity.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e206.summary: First argument that the relations designated by these names are really in God. A name and concept with nothing in reality under them are empty or false, and calling or thinking God Lord and Creator is not empty or false.
claims: Concepts without reality are false.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e209.summary: Second argument. What is only conceptual would not remain without a reasoning intellect, but God would still be Lord and Creator if no one reasoned.
claims: God would be Lord without any intellect.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e212.summary: Third argument. Every relation has its opposed correlative, and the creature's serving implies a real relation in it, so the opposite relation must be somewhere, not in the creature, which would then be its own lord and creator with opposed respects in one subject, so in God.
claims: Real servitude implies real lordship.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e216.summary: Fourth argument. Relatives without real relation are relative only by being said, like the knowable (the Philosopher), but some relatives said of God are relative by their being, like 'Lord' and 'King', so at least these signify a real relation in God.
claims: 'Lord' is relative by being.
concepts: relativa secundum esse vs. secundum dici

ta-l1d30q1-d1e219.summary: Sed contra. Nothing in God is not eternal, since whatever is in God is God, and these relations are not eternal, which is why their names are not said eternally.
claims: Whatever is in God is eternal.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e222.summary: Thomas's determination. Theologians and philosophers commonly hold that the relations by which God is referred to creatures are not in him really but only conceptually, since our intellect cannot grasp something as related to another without understanding it under the opposite relation. Reason relates to things in three ways: sometimes it apprehends what is in reality as apprehended, like the form of a stone; sometimes what is in no way in reality, like a chimera; sometimes what has some nature underlying it in reality, but not in the way it is apprehended, as the intention of genus: substance is in reality a nature not determined of itself to this or that species, and the intellect, taking one common thing from all in which the nature is found, attributes to it the character of genus, which is not in reality. So too with the relations our intellect attributes to God: it finds in him the power, essence, and operation by which the creature, having a relation to him, is produced, attributes a relation to that essence or operation, and imposes relative names according to its understanding.
claims: God's relations to creatures are of reason, but founded on his real power, essence, and operation.
Like the intention of genus, they have a real foundation but not the mode in which they are understood.
concepts: relations of reason cum fundamento in re
three relations of reason to reality

ta-l1d30q1-d1e225.summary: Reply to the first argument. Our understanding is not empty or vain, since something in reality corresponds to it, though not in the way it is in reason, as mathematical understanding is not false or vain though no line exists abstracted from matter as they consider it (the Philosopher: abstraction is not lying).
claims: Concepts with a real foundation are true though their mode is not in reality.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e231.summary: Reply to the second argument. Even if there were no intellect, there would still be in God that by which he could truly be called and understood Lord, the power to constrain subjects, but he would not be called or understood Lord in act.
claims: Without intellect God would have lordship in power, not in act.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e234.summary: Reply to the third argument. There are three kinds of relatives. In some both terms have only relations of reason, as being to non-being or relation to relation (Dist. 26). In some one term has a real relation and the other one of reason, as knowledge and the knowable. This is because the foundation is sometimes in one term only: the relation of knowledge to the knowable is founded on apprehension by spiritual being, which is in the knower and not the knowable, where the form has natural being, so the real relation is in knowledge and not in the knowable. Conversely, with lover and beloved the relation of love is founded on appetite for the good, and the good is not only in the soul but in things (the Philosopher: good and evil are in things, true and false in the soul), so Avicenna says both lover and beloved have a disposition by which they are related, unlike knower and known; so both relations are real, as with equality, founded directly on quantity in both. Since all relations of creatures to God are founded on the way they receive from God, which is not in God, since they do not attain the perfect mode by which God works in them, no real relation in God corresponds to them. But to the relation by which the Son receives from the Father there corresponds a relation in the Father, since the Father gives and the Son receives the divine nature in one and the same mode and character.
claims: Relatives may be both of reason, one real and one of reason, or both real, depending on where the foundation lies.
Creatures' relations to God have no real correlative in God; the Son's relation to the Father does.

ta-l1d30q1-d1e238.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. This is beside the point, since among both kinds of relatives some imply real relations and some relations of reason: 'same' implies a relation of reason though relative by being, and 'knowledge' a real relation though relative by being said.
claims: Relative by being vs. by being said does not track real vs. conceptual relation.
concepts: relativa secundum esse vs. secundum dici

ta-l1d30q1-d1e248.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Though he did not begin to be Lord of time from time, he began to be Lord of time' means God began to be Lord of time when time began, so as time did not begin in or from time, neither is God called Lord of time in or from time. 'In time' designates the relation of measure, as what is placed is in place as measuring it; 'from time' means time as a measure including what it measures, exceeding it on both sides, so what always is is not measured by time but what sometimes is (the Philosopher), and what is measured by time is from time, since time precedes it. Time is not measured by time, as place is not by place, so time begins neither in nor from time, but God is Lord in or from time of other things that begin so, like this or that generated thing, even if the universe had always existed. So the question does not matter, since either way God is Lord from time of at least some things. (2) The question raised in Dist. 13 is solved here: names said of God from time imply relations not real in God but conceptual and nominal, so when the Spirit is said to be given by himself, there is in the creature a real relation to the whole Trinity as principle and to the Spirit as term by way of exemplarity, but in the Spirit only a relation of reason, and nothing prevents something being referred to itself by such a relation, as the same is the same as itself.
claims: God is Lord of time not from time but as time begins; of other things he is Lord from time.
The Spirit's being given by himself involves a real relation only in the creature.

ta-l1d30q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 30 introduces names said of God from time, without change or real relation in God, and announces three articles: whether such names exist, whether they signify the essence, and whether they posit real relations in God.
claims: Temporal names imply no change in God.

ta-l1d30q1-Dd1e110.summary: Article 1 holds that some things must be said of God from time: since all being flows from God and many things have not always existed, relations of principle to them are said from time, since a relation in act requires both extremes. Relations, unlike absolute predicates, can be newly said without change in their subject. God 'becomes' only conceptually and is never changed, and temporal names are per se and eternal as to their foundation, per accidens as to the relation.
claims: Relations to creatures are said of God from time without change in him.

ta-l1d30q1-Dd1e154.summary: Article 2 holds that temporal names relating God to creatures as principle belong to the whole Trinity and signify the essence, principally ('Creator') or consequently ('Lord'). Names relating God as term, by operation, exemplarity, or being (the Incarnation), can belong to one person while including the Trinity as principle. So mission and incarnation are personal as to term and Trinitarian as to principle, and the hypostatic union is a real relation in the creature.
claims: Temporal names as principle are essential and Trinitarian; as term they can be personal.

ta-l1d30q1-Dd1e198.summary: Article 3 holds that God's relations to creatures are of reason only, though founded on his real power, essence, and operation, like the intention of genus, which has a real foundation but not the mode in which it is understood. Such concepts are not false, God would be Lord in power without any intellect, and relatives may be both conceptual, mixed, or both real depending on where the foundation lies. Creatures' relations to God have no real correlative in him, while the Son's relation to the Father does.
claims: God's relations to creatures are relations of reason with a real foundation.
Creature–God relations are mixed; Father–Son relations are mutually real.
concepts: relations of reason cum fundamento in re

ta-l1d30q1-Dd1e243.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 30 explains how God is Lord of time not from time, distinguishing 'in time' from 'from time'. It solves Lombard's earlier question about the Spirit given by himself through the real relation in the creature and the conceptual relation in the Spirit.
claims: God is Lord of time as time begins.
Relations in temporal names are real only in the creature.

ta-l1d30q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 30 treats names said of God from time. Article 1 holds that relations to creatures are said of God from time, since a relation in act needs both extremes, without any change in God, because relation posits nothing in its subject. Article 2 holds that such names signify the essence and belong to the whole Trinity when they relate God as principle. When they relate God as term, by operation, exemplarity, or the Incarnation, they can be personal. Article 3 holds that God's relations to creatures are relations of reason founded on his real power and operation, mixed relations in which only the creature's side is real, unlike the mutually real relations of Father and Son.
claims: Temporal names imply no change in God.
They signify the essence as principle and can be personal as term.
God's relations to creatures are of reason, with real foundation.
